opus-5.5.text:
I think DeepSeek was a real turning point in how investors thought about this space. Before it, the dominant story was almost purely about scale: whoever has the most GPUs and the most capital wins, and everyone else is a rounding error. A lot of investors had internalized that you basically couldn't compete with the frontier labs unless you could raise billions.

When DeepSeek came out, it showed that a relatively lean team with strong engineering taste, very good researchers, and a lot of focus on efficiency could get remarkably close to the frontier. That shook the assumption that capital alone is the moat. So the conversation shifted. Investors started asking about algorithmic insight, training efficiency, and data quality, not just compute budgets.

There were two reactions, honestly. One was a bit of panic in the public markets, the "does this mean the compute buildout is overhyped?" moment. The other, which I think was more interesting, was on the venture side. People became more open to the idea that a smaller, very talent-dense team could do something meaningful at the model level, especially in a specific domain.

For us, working on AI for mathematics, that mattered a lot. Math is a domain where you don't necessarily need to be the biggest general-purpose model. You need the right formal verification and the right data, like formal languages such as Lean, plus very strong reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. After DeepSeek, it became much easier to explain to investors why a focused team can push the frontier in reasoning without matching the hyperscalers dollar for dollar.

That said, I don't think the lesson was that compute doesn't matter. Compute still matters enormously. The lesson was that efficiency and research taste are multipliers on compute. Smart investors moved from asking "How much money can you raise?" to "What do you know that others don't, and how efficiently can you turn compute into capability?" I think that's a healthier question for the whole ecosystem.

r001.rationale: The response describes investors reconsidering compute, capital, and efficiency after DeepSeek, but does not say that being labeled an “AI model” itself became a reason not to invest.

r002.rationale: The response discusses whether capital or research efficiency creates a moat, but makes no comparison between AI models and consumer products.

fable-5.1.text:
Carina Hong: It was a real shock to the system, honestly. Before DeepSeek, the dominant narrative in the market was basically "scale is everything" — whoever has the most GPUs, the biggest cluster, the most capital, wins. And that narrative justified these enormous valuations and these enormous capex plans. Then DeepSeek comes out and shows you can get frontier-adjacent performance at a fraction of the training cost, and suddenly everyone has to ask: wait, what is the moat actually?

So in the first week or two you saw a lot of panic — Nvidia dropped, there was all this talk about whether the compute buildout was overbuilt. But I think the more thoughtful investors moved past that pretty quickly. The conclusion most people landed on was something like Jevons paradox: if intelligence gets cheaper, you use a lot more of it. Demand for compute doesn't go down, it goes up, it just shifts from training toward inference.

What changed more durably, I think, is how people think about where value accrues. If the base model is going to be commoditized — if open weights can get within striking distance of the closed labs — then raw model capability alone isn't a defensible business. So investors started asking much harder questions of model companies: what's your distribution, what's your data flywheel, what's your actual product? And conversely they got more excited about the application layer and about companies doing something genuinely differentiated on top of models, because cheaper intelligence is pure upside for them.

For us, working on AI for mathematics, it was actually encouraging. DeepSeek's reasoning work showed that reinforcement learning on verifiable domains — math, code — is where a lot of the leverage is. That's exactly the thesis we'd been building on. So we had a lot of conversations where investors who had been skeptical that a small team could matter suddenly understood that algorithmic insight and the right training signal can beat brute force. The attitude went from "you need ten billion dollars to play" to "okay, show me what you've figured out that others haven't."

r001.rationale: The candidate says investors questioned model companies’ moats and products, but does not say they treated the label “AI model” itself as a reason not to invest.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes base models as potentially commoditized, but makes no comparison between their competitive moat and that of consumer products.

astra-6.text:
My impression is that DeepSeek shifted the question investors were asking. Before, it was often, “Who can build the most powerful model, and how much capital do they need?” Afterward, it became, “If strong models can be built more efficiently, where does the lasting value sit?”

That creates two different reactions. It makes people more cautious about model companies whose advantage depends mainly on spending more. But it also makes the application layer more interesting: if intelligence gets cheaper, more products become economically viable.

So I wouldn’t describe it as investors becoming less excited about AI. It’s more that they’re scrutinizing the business model—what makes a company defensible, why customers will stay, and whether technical progress translates into durable revenue.

sol-6.1.text:
My sense was that DeepSeek made investors rethink where the value in AI would accumulate. If highly capable models could be developed more efficiently, then spending more on training wasn’t necessarily a durable competitive advantage. That put pressure on the idea that a handful of model companies would capture most of the value.

At the same time, cheaper models could make the application market much bigger. So I’d describe the reaction as a reassessment: more scrutiny of model economics, and more interest in businesses that turn those models into useful products.

r001.rationale: The response describes greater scrutiny of model economics and questions whether training spend creates a durable advantage, but does not say investors treated the “AI model” label itself as a reason not to invest.

r002.rationale: It questions models’ competitive advantage, but makes no comparison between their moat and that of consumer products.
